criteria.name: Recipient-specific opening hook
criteria.description: The email opens with a concrete, specific reference to the recipient — something they've done, backed, or care about — not a generic greeting or thesis statement.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLM cold outreach emails frequently open with pleasantries or a self-introduction/thesis; requiring a verifiable recipient-specific hook before any company description is a distinctive preference.

criteria.name: One hard number in the first three lines
criteria.description: Traction or scale is proven with a concrete quantitative data point early — no adjectives standing in for numbers.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLM cold outreach drafts often rely on vague descriptors like "strong traction" or bury numbers later; requiring a concrete metric in the first three lines is a distinctive constraint.

criteria.name: No hedging or vague alignment language
criteria.description: The email avoids soft, non-committal phrases and generic thesis-fit claims that signal the sender hasn't done specific homework.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLM cold outreach emails to investors routinely include hedging ("I believe," "we think") and generic thesis-fit language; banning both is a distinctive stylistic constraint.

criteria.name: Founder voice, not banker voice
criteria.description: Descriptions of the business use plain English that a human would actually say — not finance or consulting jargon.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLM cold emails to investors typically lean heavily on VC/consulting jargon ("go-to-market", "thesis-aligned"), so explicitly forbidding this in favor of plain mechanism-level description is a distinctive preference.

criteria.name: First-name, low-ceremony register
criteria.description: The email uses first-name address and skips formal salutations and sign-offs that create distance.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs typically default to more formal salutations ("Dear Mr. Smith") and longer, more deferential meeting requests in investor outreach, so first-name address with a terse time-boxed ask is a distinctive register choice.

rubric_raw.coaching_notes: Non-negotiables: recipient-specific opener + one hard number in first three lines + no hedging. The user reads VC cold emails constantly and treats any phrase that sounds templated as a tune-out signal — default politeness rituals actively hurt the email. criteria.name: Phenomenon-first ordering
criteria.description: Intros open by naming the specific phenomenon or pathology, then move to the explanation/trace, then the fix. The observable problem comes before the mechanism account.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLM intros for ML blog posts typically open with broad context or motivation before naming the specific pathology; enforcing a strict phenomenon-first, then-mechanism, then-fix order is a distinctive structural choice.

criteria.name: Mechanism-level specificity in the opener
criteria.description: The opener names the specific technical mechanism the work touches, not the general field or category. No framing in terms of the broad area's importance.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs typically open technical blog posts with broad field-importance framing ("LLMs have transformed..."), so requiring a mechanism-level opener with no such framing is a distinctive constraint.

criteria.name: No marketing register
criteria.description: Zero tolerance for hype phrasing, reader-flattery, or suspense-building language. The voice is a researcher reporting findings, not a marketer selling them.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLM drafts of technical blog intros frequently include mild hype words ("groundbreaking", "cutting-edge") and reader-engagement hooks; a zero-tolerance ban on these is a distinctive stylistic constraint.

criteria.name: Explicit signposting of the payoff
criteria.description: The intro tells the reader concretely what artifacts (tables, figures, results) to expect later in the post. Short, plain pointers, not teases.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLM intros for ML blog posts typically use teaser hooks or general motivation rather than concretely naming specific tables/figures/results readers will encounter.

criteria.name: Researcher-as-author voice
criteria.description: The prose sounds like it was written by someone who actually did the work — confident, terse, technically precise claims with ownership ('we trace', 'we show'), not third-party summary or promotional framing.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLM drafts of ML blog intros frequently include promotional framing like "in this post we dive into" and hedged buildup; requiring terse first-person ownership without such framing is a distinctive voice constraint.

fixtures.genre: Slack status update (engineering manager to team)

criteria.name: Names the technical root cause
criteria.description: Status updates must identify the actual technical reason for the state being reported, not abstract it into 'challenges' or 'issues'. The team is technical and wants the mechanism.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLM drafts of status updates tend to use vague phrases like "ran into issues" or "unforeseen challenges"; requiring a named mechanism and where it was caught is a distinctive technical-directness preference.

criteria.name: Ends on the number or date that matters
criteria.description: The final line should be the single piece of information the team most needs to walk away with — typically a date, version, or quantity. No generic sign-offs or calls for questions.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs typically end Slack updates with "let me know if you have questions" or similar closers; ending on a bare number/date with no sign-off is a distinctive user preference.

criteria.name: Lowercase, Slack-native styling
criteria.description: Written in all lowercase with the rhythm of someone typing in Slack. No title-case headers, no formal capitalization of sentence starts.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs default to sentence-case capitalization and often include salutations even in Slack contexts; enforcing all-lowercase with fragment rhythm is a distinctive stylistic preference.

criteria.name: No corporate/press-release register
criteria.description: Cuts phrasing that sounds like leadership comms: reassurances of commitment, abstract gestures at 'working on solutions', framing sentences that don't carry new information.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs routinely include preamble ("I wanted to update you on...") and reassuring framing sentences in status updates, so banning these is a distinctive user preference.

criteria.name: Respects what the team already knows
criteria.description: Doesn't restate context, project names, or background that the team already has. Treats readers as insiders.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs tend to add context/background and use formal project names defensively; explicitly treating readers as insiders and using team shorthand is a distinctive preference.

fixtures.name: weak_product_blurb
fixtures.genre: short product description for a landing page

criteria.name: Quantitative-result opener
criteria.description: The first line leads with a concrete, quantified outcome for the user rather than an abstract capability statement. Numbers do the persuasive work up front.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLM product descriptions typically open with abstract capability/benefit statements ("Streamline your workflow..."), not a quantified user outcome in the first sentence.

criteria.name: Customer social proof
criteria.description: The blurb includes named customer logos or mentions to establish credibility, not just capability claims.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs typically write capability-focused product blurbs without inventing or including named customer logos, and wouldn't default to a closing "used by" credibility line.

dimensions.label: First sentence contains a specific number or percentage
dimensions.evidence: Message #8: assistant selected the variant opening 'Ship faster with 90% less time spent writing tests' over 'Automate your test coverage,' arguing the concrete metric was stronger; user accepted in Message #9.
dimensions.judge_reasoning:
TRANSFERABLE
Applies to any product description regardless of the product; the rule about including a specific number/percentage is a reusable pattern.

dimensions.label: Opener frames a user outcome (time saved, bugs caught, speed) rather than what the product does
dimensions.evidence: Message #8: assistant contrasted outcome-led '90% less time' against capability-led 'Automate your test coverage' and user accepted the outcome-led choice in Message #9.
dimensions.judge_reasoning:
TRANSFERABLE
This describes a reusable pattern (outcome-first framing) that applies to any product description, with parenthetical examples rather than locked-in specifics.

dimensions.label: Does not open with an abstract imperative like 'automate', 'streamline', 'transform'
dimensions.evidence: Message #8: the abstract-verb opener ('Automate your test coverage') was explicitly rejected in favor of the quantified one; user agreed in Message #9.
dimensions.judge_reasoning:
TRANSFERABLE
This negative constraint applies to any product description regardless of the product, checking for a common vague-imperative opener.

dimensions.label: Includes a 'used by' line naming specific customers
dimensions.evidence: Message #6: variant included 'Used by teams at [Customer], [Customer], and [Customer]'; user accepted this variant as final in Messages #7–9.
dimensions.judge_reasoning:
TRANSFERABLE
Applies to any landing page product description; the specific customer names vary but the rule (include a social-proof line) is reusable.

dimensions.label: Social proof appears as a closing credibility line, not in the opener
dimensions.evidence: Message #6: customer names were placed at the end after the value prop; user accepted this structure in Message #9.
dimensions.judge_reasoning:
TRANSFERABLE
This describes a structural placement rule that applies to any product description regardless of the specific product or social proof content.

fixtures.name: weak_birthday_card
fixtures.genre: birthday card message for a coworker

criteria.name: Stays brief over personalized
criteria.description: For acquaintance-level coworker greetings, the user prefers a short generic note over anything that adds personal detail or extended warmth. When offered the choice between adding personalization and keeping it brief, they choose brief.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs typically try to add warmth, personalization prompts, or distinctive voice in birthday messages; explicitly preferring brief and generic over personalized is a distinguishing user preference.

dimensions.label: Body of the note is no more than three short sentences
dimensions.evidence: Message #1: user asked for a 'short' note; Message #5: user confirmed 'Brief is fine' when offered the chance to add more.
dimensions.judge_reasoning:
TRANSFERABLE
This length constraint applies to any birthday card message regardless of the coworker or topic.

dimensions.label: Does not invent specific personal details about the recipient (hobbies, inside references, specific shared memories)

dimensions.judge_reasoning:
TRANSFERABLE
This rule applies to any birthday card for any coworker; it prohibits fabrication without referencing specific people or details.

criteria.name: Minimal field set
criteria.description: Report includes only the fields needed to act on the bug. No placeholder sections, no optional metadata slots (screenshots, tags, priority labels) unless the user explicitly asks for them.
criteria.judge_reasoning:
SPECIFIC
Baseline LLMs typically include rich scaffolding (priority, labels, attachments placeholders, tags) when drafting bug reports, so restricting to a minimal field set is a distinctive user preference.

dimensions.evidence: Message #5: user declined a screenshot placeholder with 'No, this is enough.'
dimensions.judge_reasoning:
TRANSFERABLE
This rule applies to any bug report regardless of the specific bug or placeholder content.

dimensions.label: No priority/label/tag fields added unless requested
dimensions.evidence: Message #5: user declined priority tags when offered.
dimensions.judge_reasoning:
TRANSFERABLE
This rule applies to any bug report regardless of topic; it constrains behavior without referencing specific content.

dimensions.label: Sticks to repro, expected, actual, severity, environment without extra scaffolding

dimensions.judge_reasoning:
TRANSFERABLE
The label describes a structural rule (standard bug report fields) that applies to any bug ticket regardless of the specific defect.
